prize_parts.citation: For showing how collateral constraints link credit limits to asset prices, so that small shocks are amplified and propagated into persistent macroeconomic downturns.

statement.case_for: I keep B004 as my preferred part but narrow the credited names from the round-1 trio to the Kiyotaki-Moore pair. Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) supply a formal and tractable mechanism. When claims on future cash flows cannot be fully pledged, a durable collateralisable asset ties borrowing capacity to asset prices, and the feedback turns a small shock into a persistent downturn. This is the macro counterpart of the incomplete-contracting logic I know from corporate finance, which is why I can judge the conceptual step with some confidence. It has about three decades of extension and use, and the 2007-09 crisis tested its relevance, so maturity is not in question. Attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist. Two people originated a single mechanism, and every colleague who discussed B004 treats them as the core. The round-1 exchange moved me on Gertler. Nobody showed that his intermediary-finance credit can be separated from the Bernanke-Gertler accelerator strand, which the 2022 prize touched, or from his place on B015. Hassler proposed the pair in his opening, Boppart now finds the pair easier to defend, and Andersson holds the Gertler credit less firmly. I would prefer a defensible narrow citation to a broader one whose third name I cannot defend. On the chair's request for a common weighting, I weight identification quality, conceptual originality, maturity and attribution tractability roughly equally. On that basis I order B004 (pair), then B027, then B002, with B015 behind them because of its attribution cost. I give this ordering separately from my fallback preferences.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that a pair leaves the quantitative and intermediary-balance-sheet strand uncredited. That strand is arguably what carried the mechanism into post-2008 policy models, and Hassler is right that the Committee should say so explicitly. Marginal novelty relative to the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises is also a fair question, although that prize concerned bank runs, intermediation and the Depression, not collateral-driven credit cycles in macro models. The aggregate evidence for the mechanism is mostly calibrated or indirect, not cleanly identified, and Gilchrist's empirical work is left out. Finally, B002 and B027 have broader opening first-place support. I do not treat that as scientific merit, but I cannot ignore that B004 is unlikely to reach six votes without shifts. My familiarity with financial contracting could also make me overrate this mechanism.

responses.point: Hassler proposed only Kiyotaki and Moore for B004. He noted that a two-name award leaves the financial-accelerator strand uncredited and that the Committee should be explicit about that. He also argued that the 2022 prize leaves B004 with less marginal novelty than B015.
responses.response: I now take your pair. On the explicitness point I agree and would say it plainly: the pair credits the collateral-constraint mechanism and does not credit the accelerator or the intermediary strand. That is a deliberate narrowing, and the citation is worded to match. On novelty I still disagree. The 2022 prize concerned bank runs, intermediation and the Depression, whereas B004 is about how pledgeable collateral links asset prices and credit limits to aggregate fluctuations, and it contains no overlap in the core mechanism. I accept that the overlap is stronger for Gertler's credit than for the pair, which is the reason for the change.

responses.point: Andersson shares my B004 trio. He holds the Gertler inclusion less firmly and says the pair would be the better citation if the Gertler credit is hard to separate from Bernanke's. He also argues that the mechanism's absorption into crisis analysis is evidence of lasting importance.
responses.response: I agree with the last point, and it is the same reason I treat maturity as settled for B004. On Gertler, you and I both named him as the weakest part of our configuration, and the exchange gave no argument that resolves it. Neither of us has shown that the intermediary-finance strand is separable from the accelerator credit. So I am moving to the pair, and I hope you will state in the vote discussion whether you accept that, since the chair has asked. I would not call the move a retreat from the science. It follows from not being able to defend the exact credit of a third name.

responses.point: Fredriksson does not find B004 clearly stronger than B027 on novelty, because he sees the 2022 prize as overlapping substantially with the financial-frictions agenda. He also asks that the 2024 prize enter as a timing consideration and not a scientific one.
responses.response: I agree on the 2024 prize and apply the same standard to the 2022 one: both are timing considerations and not evidence about merit. On the substance I think the overlap is real for the Bernanke-Gertler accelerator but much weaker for Kiyotaki-Moore, which is part of why I narrowed to the pair. B027 remains my first alternative. I accept your point that its credit is concentrated and its maturity is greater than that of B002. The identification gap you concede for cross-country evidence is the main reason I do not rank it above B004.

responses.point: Teorell prefers B027 and distinguishes it from the 2024 institutions prize: that prize concerned the origins of institutions, while B027 takes institutions as given and asks how rules shape policy. He accepts that identification is weaker than in design-based work and sees Besley as complementary rather than central.
responses.response: Your distinction persuades me that the 2024 prize is not a scientific obstacle for B027. I raised proximity only as a timing question. Your own comment on Besley matters for the comparison. If the pair is the clean core in B027, as you and Fredriksson say, then my B004 move is symmetrical, and the two parts are on the same footing for attribution. This leaves identification and breadth of policy use as the main differences between us. I weigh the macro-financial mechanism's policy use and post-2008 confirmation more heavily, while you weigh the field-creating framework. I do not think either weighting is wrong, and I do not want the vote to blur that difference.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B002 first. She holds that the neighbourhood and exposure evidence has been extended with other administrative datasets and that the unresolved question concerns the size of specific causal effects. She would have the citation stay close to what is established.
responses.response: That is a fair distinction and it moves me slightly on B002. The measurement advance and the exposure-based designs look durable, and a citation limited to them would address most of my maturity worry. I remain cautious on timing: replication in non-US data and long-run follow-up are the evidence I would want before ranking it above a mechanism with three decades of testing. I therefore keep it as the second alternative. My hesitation is about the order of candidates and not about the quality of the work.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee finds Gertler's intermediary-finance contribution separable from the 2022-recognised accelerator strand. If it does, the trio would restore a strand that the pair omits.
Whether the Committee regards the 2022 prize as having covered the financial-frictions agenda, or sees collateral-driven credit cycles as a distinct discovery.
How much weight a mechanism with mostly calibrated or indirect aggregate evidence should carry, and whether Gilchrist's empirical work should be credited.
Whether the long-run causal evidence on B002 and the identification gap on B027 should change the order of these alternatives.
My assessments rely on general knowledge of the literature and the supplied files, not on independent verification of citations.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile: no listed co-author or institutional connection with Kiyotaki, Moore or Gertler, and none with the credited names in B027 or B002. My research on financial contracting and incomplete-contracts theory is adjacent to the collateral-constraint literature, and I chaired the Committee in 2016-2018, so familiarity may bias my view. I also hold the KVA Vice President role since 2024. My profile records a long committee overlap with Hassler, Krusell, Ellingsen and Svensson, which I disclose without treating it as agreement. I disclose these items and do not adjudicate them.
